title: Cut marks on mammoth bones suggest Ice Age hunters killed the giants at Breitenbach
dek: New finds at Germany's largest Aurignacian open-air site challenge the idea that early humans only scavenged ancient ivory. The evidence points to active hunting 30,000 years ago.
body: In July and October 2026, archaeologists uncovered more than 2,000 finds at Breitenbach-Schneidemühle in southern Saxony-Anhalt. Among them were dense concentrations of mammoth bones, large tusk fragments and worked ivory. Most strikingly, several bones bear cut marks that the team argues indicate butchery. If confirmed, this would be the first direct evidence that the site's inhabitants hunted mammoths rather than collecting fossil ivory from the landscape.

Breitenbach covers roughly 10,000 square metres, making it the largest known open-air Aurignacian settlement in western Eurasia. The Aurignacian culture, dated broadly from 42,000 to 32,000 years ago, marks the early expansion of anatomically modern humans across Europe. Most sites from this period are caves or rock shelters. A preserved open-air camp of this scale lets researchers map how people organised living and working spaces, not just what they ate or made.

Earlier research had suggested the ivory worked at Breitenbach was significantly older than the human occupation, dated to roughly 32,000 to 34,000 years ago. Dr Olaf Jöris of MONREPOS, part of the Leibniz Centre for Archaeology, said previous investigations indicated the ivory likely came from fossil or subfossil remains collected from the surrounding area. That interpretation shaped the view that Breitenbach's people were ivory scavengers, not mammoth hunters.

Animal remains from the site tell a clear story about daily diet. Reindeer were the primary prey. Horses were taken less often and red deer only occasionally. Foxes and hares were also exploited, probably for their fur. Mammoths were absent from this dietary picture until the 2026 excavation revealed the new bone concentrations with cut marks. The marks suggest carcasses were processed for meat, while tusks supplied raw ivory and hides may have been used for clothing or shelter.

The site's layout reinforces the picture of a complex, organised camp. Researchers have identified specialised activity areas, including an ivory workshop littered with manufacturing debris, finished beads, projectile points and fragments of carved figurines. Ivory was not merely a practical material. It was shaped into weapons, tools, jewellery and art, offering a glimpse of symbolic life more than 30,000 years ago. Distinct zones for processing Arctic fox and mountain hare pelts have also been mapped.

Breitenbach's archaeological history stretches back a century. A schoolboy found a mammoth tooth during sawmill construction in 1924. Three years later, Swedish archaeologist Dr Nils Niklasson directed the first extensive excavations, investigating nearly 400 square metres. The mammoth remains recovered in 2026 are the first large concentrations found since Niklasson's campaign. Modern work resumed in 2009 through a joint project by MONREPOS and Saxony-Anhalt's State Office for Heritage Management and Archaeology, with more than 150 additional square metres excavated using current techniques.

The new finds could add a missing dimension to the site's story. The combination of exceptional preservation, specialised workshops and thousands of artefacts already allows an unusually detailed reconstruction of daily Aurignacian life. If the cut marks withstand further analysis, they would show that Breitenbach's inhabitants confronted, killed and butchered one of the Ice Age's largest animals, not just gathered its ancient remains.
doesnt_show: The cut marks have not yet been confirmed by detailed microscopic analysis to rule out natural abrasion or carnivore damage. The exact number of mammoths represented and whether they were killed at the site or brought there as carcasses remains undetermined.
settle: Microscopic analysis of the cut marks and spatial study of the bone distributions would clarify whether mammoths were hunted on site or scavenged.
